\S\ref{subsec:dist-shift} showed that exposure bias selectively destroys GAR-ours while GAR-Dongre remains unaffected under standard training. We test whether this selectivity extends beyond attention with Turn-level Residual Coherence (TRC), the cosine similarity between hidden states at the last-token position of adjacent assistant turns. For ThreadGate, TF/AR TRC is 0.334/0.332 (gap $+$0.002); for LoRA-only, 0.349/0.411 (gap $-$0.062, reversed). Neither shows a gap comparable to the GAR collapse, confirming that exposure bias disrupts a specific routing behavior (summary-position attention to goal tokens) while leaving internal representations intact.

Cross-model evaluation extends this selectivity: GAR-Dongre shows negligible distribution shift on both Llama-3.1-8B (AR/TF ratio 1.002$\times$) and Qwen-2.5-7B (1.28$\times$), compared to the order-of-magnitude collapse in GAR-ours (the scheduled sampling experiment in \S\ref{sec:discussion} breaks this pattern, with GAR-Dongre rising to 0.353).

To test whether the failure generalizes, we replicate on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \citep{grattafiori2024llama3} with Base, ThreadGate, and LoRA-only. Phase~1 diagnostics confirm goal attention decay (GAR: 0.026$\to$0.003 over 10 turns). Teacher-forced GAR-ours ($N$\,=\,50) is 0.484 (TG) and 0.481 (LoRA-only); gating contributes zero benefit. We report both mean and median GAR-ours for autoregressive evaluation. The AR distribution is heavy-tailed (CoV\,$>$\,100\%; 5--8\% of turn-level measurements exhibit sporadic attention spikes), making the median more representative. Median GAR-ours ($N$\,=\,20 mid-turn conversations, excluding the first two turns) is 0.018 for both TG and LoRA-only (Base: 0.009), yielding TF-AR gaps of 27$\times$ and 26$\times$; mean GAR-ours is 0.043 (TG) and 0.028 (LoRA-only), yielding gaps of 11$\times$ and 17$\times$ respectively, as outlier spikes (5\% of TG turns with GAR\,$\geq$\,0.4) inflate the mean. The TF-AR gap is substantial on both architectures (8--17$\times$ on Qwen, 27$\times$ by median on Llama), consistent with the exposure bias hypothesis. The gate profile differs---Qwen's minimum at layers~3--4, Llama's at layer~25---yet both converge toward identity under NTP pressure (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-llama}).

Table~\ref{tab:four-way} presents the five-way comparison. Under teacher-forced evaluation, all four fine-tuned variants converge to nearly identical performance: GAR-ours spans only 0.75 percentage points (pp) across configurations (0.50--0.51), and PPL is 2.78 for all four on IID evaluation.

The Base model confirms that LoRA fine-tuning is the operative variable: GAR-ours jumps from 0.01 to ${\sim}$0.50, while PPL improves from 4.23 to 2.78. Since all four variants share the same GAR loss ($\tau = 0.5$), convergence near the target is expected and does not demonstrate gating benefit. We cannot exclude LoRA capacity saturation at rank~16, though uniform convergence across four architecturally distinct variants makes this unlikely. GAR-Dongre remains uniformly low (0.01--0.02) across all standard-trained conditions, consistent with \citet{dongre2026attention}; a preliminary scheduled sampling experiment breaks this pattern (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Under autoregressive generation ($N$\,=\,50), GAR-ours drops to 0.019--0.064, an 8--17$\times$ gap from teacher-forced performance. Turn-conditioned gating (ThreadGate) provides statistically significant improvement over LoRA-only (Wilcoxon $p$\,=\,0.004, $r$\,=\,0.454; GAR-ours 0.064 vs 0.037; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-stats}), yet the residual gap remains large (7.8$\times$), confirming exposure bias as the dominant barrier rather than gating architecture. A second ThreadGate seed (123) confirms TF stability: GAR-ours $0.504\pm0.001$, identical PPL. We analyze this distribution shift in \S\ref{sec:analysis}.

All training-time interventions leave the exposure bias gap largely intact. We test whether inference-time attention manipulation can recover GAR by applying an additive bias $\beta$ to goal-token attention logits at every layer of the ThreadGate checkpoint during generation.

An initial sweep on $N$\,=\,5 ten-turn conversations (Figure~\ref{fig:steering}a) reveals a sharp nonlinearity between $\beta$\,=\,2 and $\beta$\,=\,5: GAR increases ${\sim}$11$\times$ (0.062\,$\to$\,0.6795$\pm$0.020) while PPL rises 35\% (1.41\,$\to$\,1.91). At $\beta$\,=\,10, GAR saturates at 0.959 but PPL degrades to 4.22.

$N$\,=\,50 conversations from a held-out evaluation set (39 with $\geq$3 turns, mean 3.6 user turns; Figure~\ref{fig:steering}b) confirm the qualitative steering pattern observed in the $N$\,=\,5 pilot (10 turns each), with consistent nonlinearity range and saturation behavior. A finer $\beta$ sweep localizes the nonlinearity: GAR jumps from 0.128$\pm$0.110 ($\beta$\,=\,2) to 0.556$\pm$0.060 ($\beta$\,=\,3), an 8.7$\times$ recovery from baseline with only 9\% PPL increase (1.43\,$\to$\,1.56), identifying $\beta$\,=\,3 as a practical operating point. The $\beta$\,=\,0 distribution is right-skewed (mean 0.064, median 0.031, std 0.081), driven by short conversations with high baseline GAR; absolute baselines therefore differ from the 10-turn $N$\,=\,5 evaluation (0.028). At $\beta$\,=\,5, GAR reaches 0.727$\pm$0.061 with PPL 1.77$\pm$0.27, confirming the recovery pattern at scale (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-steering}).

These results provide constructive evidence that attention misallocation---not representation degradation---is a proximal cause of exposure-bias-induced GAR failure under the tested conditions (Qwen-2.5-7B, UltraChat, GAR-family losses): manually correcting attention via $\beta$ bias restores GAR, and inference-time intervention circumvents the exposure bias barrier. This steering experiment is diagnostic: it requires identifying goal tokens, trivial for system prompts but not generalizable.

An initial sweep ($N$\,=\,5, 10-turn; Figure~\ref{fig:steering}a) reveals sharp nonlinearity: GAR increases ${\sim}$11$\times$ at $\beta$\,=\,5 (0.062$\to$0.680) with 35\% PPL rise; at $\beta$\,=\,10, GAR saturates (0.959) but PPL degrades to 4.22. At $\beta$\,=\,5, GAR reaches 0.727$\pm$0.061 (PPL 1.77; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-steering}).

This provides constructive evidence that attention misallocation---not representation degradation---is the proximal cause: manually correcting attention restores GAR, circumventing the exposure bias barrier. The experiment is diagnostic, requiring goal-token identification.

\paragraph{Exposure bias.}
Teacher forcing creates a distributional mismatch between training and inference that compounds over sequence length \citep{wiseman2016sequence,arora2022exposure}. Scheduled Sampling \citep{bengio2015scheduled} introduced curriculum-based mixing of ground-truth and model-generated tokens. \section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The failure traces to an incompatibility between teacher-forcing and GAR-family auxiliary losses, not to the gating architecture. NTP gradient pressure (7.5--14.7$\times$ the GAR magnitude) pushes gates toward identity (2--7\% attenuation). Inference-time steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR from 0.064 to 0.727, providing constructive evidence that attention misallocation is a proximal cause (\S\ref{subsec:steering}).

\paragraph{Scheduled sampling confirms exposure bias.} Scheduled sampling \citep{bengio2015scheduled} mixes teacher-forced and model-generated contexts during training, increasing AR GAR-ours from 0.064 to 0.347 (5.4$\times$) and compressing the 7.8$\times$ gap to 1.44$\times$ with negligible PPL change (1.44 vs.\ 1.43); a second seed yields 0.418 (gap 1.20$\times$). GAR-Dongre also rises (0.019$\to$0.353). By directly targeting the train-inference mismatch, this implicates exposure bias as the dominant factor; the gating benefit diminishes in longer dialogues (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-n5}), consistent with compounding over turns.

\paragraph{Downstream effects.} KV cache drift---model-generated key-value states diverging from teacher-forced statistics---is a downstream consequence of exposure bias rather than an independent cause; disentangling requires a switching experiment (future work). Instruction retention evaluation ($\beta$\,=\,3, 18 constraint types) shows content compliance rising +23.8\,pp ($p$\,=\,0.077) with GAR correlation $r$\,=\,0.200 ($p$\,=\,0.007), while format constraints show no change (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ir}).

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Setup}
5	
6	We fine-tune Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct on 8K multi-turn conversations from the UltraChat training split. Training uses 3 epochs with AdamW (lr $= 2 \times 10^{-4}$, batch size 1, gradient accumulation 8, seed 42; ThreadGate additionally with seed 123); each variant requires approximately 6 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (102\,GB). Full hyperparameters are in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-hyper}; the controlled comparison design is described in \S\ref{sec:comparison-design}. We evaluate under \emph{IID} (same-distribution UltraChat text) and \emph{held-out} (50 non-overlapping conversations) teacher-forced protocols, reporting GAR-ours, GAR-Dongre \citep{dongre2026attention}, and PPL.
7	
8	\subsection{Main Results}
9	
10	Table~\ref{tab:four-way} presents the five-way comparison. Under TF evaluation, all four fine-tuned variants converge: GAR-ours spans 0.75\,pp (0.50--0.51), PPL is 2.78 for all. The Base model confirms LoRA fine-tuning as the operative variable (GAR-ours: 0.01$\to$${\sim}$0.50). Convergence near $\tau$\,=\,0.5 is expected given the shared GAR loss and does not demonstrate gating benefit. GAR-Dongre remains low (0.01--0.02); scheduled sampling breaks this pattern (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
11	
12	Under AR generation ($N$\,=\,50), GAR-ours drops to 0.019--0.064, an 8--17$\times$ gap. ThreadGate significantly outperforms LoRA-only (Wilcoxon $p$\,=\,0.004, $r$\,=\,0.454; GAR-ours 0.064 vs 0.037; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-stats}), yet the residual gap remains large (7.8$\times$). A second seed (123) confirms TF stability ($0.504\pm0.001$). We analyze this distribution shift in \S\ref{sec:analysis}.
13	
14	\begin{table*}[t]

(a)~Initial evaluation ($N$\,=\,5, 10-turn conversations): sharp increase at $\beta \in [2, 5]$, GAR ${\sim}$11$\times$ recovery with 35\% PPL rise. (b)~Larger-scale evaluation ($N$\,=\,50, 39 with $\geq$3 turns, mean 3.6 user turns) with finer $\beta$ sweep: the nonlinearity localizes between $\beta$\,=\,2 and $\beta$\,=\,3, identifying $\beta$\,=\,3 as a practical operating point (8.7$\times$ GAR recovery, 9\% PPL cost). High-$\beta$ results are consistent across sample sizes. Dotted line: unsteered teacher-forced baseline.}

lines: Table~\ref{tab:four-way} presents the five-way comparison. Under TF evaluation, all four fine-tuned variants converge: GAR-ours spans 0.75\,pp (0.50--0.51), PPL is 2.78 for all. The Base model confirms LoRA fine-tuning as the operative variable (GAR-ours: 0.01$\to$${\sim}$0.50). Convergence near $\tau$\,=\,0.5 is expected given the shared GAR loss and does not demonstrate gating benefit. GAR-Dongre remains low (0.01--0.02); scheduled sampling breaks this pattern (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

-Under AR generation ($N$\,=\,50), GAR-ours drops to 0.019--0.064, an 8--17$\times$ gap. ThreadGate significantly outperforms LoRA-only (Wilcoxon $p$\,=\,0.004, $r$\,=\,0.454; GAR-ours 0.064 vs 0.037; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-stats}), yet the residual gap remains large (7.8$\times$). A second seed (123) confirms TF stability ($0.504\pm0.001$). We analyze this distribution shift in \S\ref{sec:analysis}.

+Under AR generation ($N$\,=\,50), GAR-ours drops to 0.019--0.064, an 8--17$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:training-dynamics}). ThreadGate significantly outperforms LoRA-only (Wilcoxon $p$\,=\,0.004, $r$\,=\,0.454; GAR-ours 0.064 vs 0.037; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-stats}), yet the residual gap remains large (7.8$\times$). A second seed (123) confirms TF stability ($0.504\pm0.001$). We analyze this distribution shift in \S\ref{sec:analysis}.

1	\section{Training Configuration}\label{sec:appendix-hyper}
2	
3	Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} lists the full training configuration shared across all fine-tuned variants. ThreadGate gate parameters receive a $10\times$ learning rate multiplier and are initialized with bias 1.5 ($\sigma(1.5) \approx 0.82$); the gate MLP adds ${\sim}$57K parameters per variant ($<$0.001\% of 7B). The scheduled sampling variant (v8b) linearly increases the model-generated context ratio from 0 to 0.5 over 3 epochs (29.7--37.1\% effective usage due to per-sample Bernoulli sampling). All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (102\,GB VRAM), requiring 6--8 hours per variant.
4

35	\section{Loss Formulation Search}\label{sec:appendix-loss}
36	
37	The final MSE + gate diversity loss (\S\ref{sec:loss}) emerged from seven iterations spanning four loss families. Table~\ref{tab:loss-iterations} summarizes the progression. The search was motivated by a consistent failure mode: naive formulations either collapse to trivial solutions (cumulative losses) or drive gates toward identity (maximize-family losses). We describe each family below.
38	
39	\paragraph{Cumulative losses (v1--v2).} These losses accumulate GAR contributions across layers, rewarding monotonically increasing attention. v1 collapsed because once the cumulative GAR exceeded the threshold, the loss gradient vanished and gates froze. v2 added an $\varepsilon$-stabilization term to the cumulative product, but numerical instability from the product of 28 per-layer terms dominated, and training followed the same trajectory.
40	
41	\paragraph{Maximize losses (v3--v5).} These losses directly maximize mean GAR ($-\text{mean}(\text{GAR})$). The unbounded objective rewards full pass-through ($g \to 1.0$), collapsing gate diversity (std $<$ 0.025). At $\lambda$=2 (v3), gates froze within 100 steps; at $\lambda$=10 (v3b), convergence to identity accelerated; at $\lambda$=1 (v5), rebalancing delayed but did not prevent the same degenerate solution.
42	
43	\paragraph{Smooth saturation (v6).} This bounded the reward using a saturating function, intended to prevent the unbounded growth of maximize losses. In practice, the loss landscape remained monotonic in $g$, and training followed the same terminal trajectory as the maximize family, only more slowly.
44	
45	\paragraph{MSE + gate diversity (v7).} The MSE formulation provides bidirectional pressure: GAR above $\tau$ incurs the same penalty as GAR below $\tau$, preventing the runaway optimization of maximize losses. The gate diversity regularizer ($\mathcal{L}_\text{div}$) enforces a minimum standard deviation across per-layer gate values, preventing all gates from collapsing to a uniform value. This combination is the only one that achieved stable convergence (GAR-ours = 0.50, PPL = 2.78).
46

66	\section{Instruction Retention Details}\label{sec:appendix-ir}
67	
68	To evaluate whether GAR improvements translate to downstream task performance, we test instruction retention across 18 system-prompt constraint types using the ThreadGate checkpoint with $\beta$\,=\,3 steering. Each constraint type requires the model to follow a specific instruction embedded in the system prompt (e.g., ``always respond in bullet points'', ``never use the word X'', ``include a summary at the end'').
69	
70	Table~\ref{tab:ir-results} reports per-category compliance rates. Content constraints---which require attending to and recalling specific system-prompt instructions---show the largest improvement (+23.8\,pp), consistent with GAR measuring attention to goal tokens. Format and count constraints, which are more procedural and less dependent on sustained attention to the system prompt, show no change.
71	
72	The GAR-compliance correlation ($r$\,=\,0.200, $p$\,=\,0.007) is statistically significant but modest, suggesting that attention to goal tokens is one of several factors in instruction compliance. McNemar's test ($p$\,=\,0.077) is marginally significant for the overall compliance improvement, reflecting the small sample size (18 constraint types). These results are exploratory and pending multi-model confirmation.

93	
94	The main results (Table~\ref{tab:four-way}) report AR GAR from $N$\,=\,50 held-out conversations with a mean of 3.6 user turns. Table~\ref{tab:n5-ar} presents complementary results on $N$\,=\,5 conversations with 10 turns each. In these longer dialogues, the gating advantage observed in shorter conversations vanishes: all fine-tuned variants collapse to AR GAR-ours of 0.015--0.025, compared to 0.030--0.064 in the shorter evaluation. This length dependence is consistent with exposure bias compounding over turns---each model-generated turn introduces additional distributional drift from the teacher-forced training regime, and by turn 10 the accumulated drift overwhelms any gating signal.

114	\section{Statistical Test Details}\label{sec:appendix-stats}
115	
116	All statistical tests reported in the main text use non-parametric methods due to the non-normal, heavy-tailed distribution of per-conversation GAR values. Table~\ref{tab:stat-tests} consolidates the full results.
117	
118	\paragraph{Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.} We use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for all pairwise configuration comparisons under AR evaluation, treating each conversation as a paired observation. The TG vs.\ LoRA-only comparison ($p$\,=\,0.004, $r$\,=\,0.454) confirms that turn-conditioned gating provides a statistically significant but modest improvement. The TG vs.\ +PCGrad comparison ($p$\,=\,0.002) shows that resolving gradient conflict is actively harmful. Gate turn conditioning uses an unpaired Wilcoxon test across 28 layers.
119	
120	\paragraph{Bootstrap confidence intervals.} The 95\% CIs in Table~\ref{tab:four-way} are computed via 10,000 bootstrap resamples of per-conversation mid-turn GAR averages (turns 2--$T$), using the percentile method.
121	
122	\paragraph{Effect sizes.} We report rank-biserial correlation $r = Z / \sqrt{N}$ as the effect size for Wilcoxon tests, where $Z$ is the standardized test statistic and $N$ is the number of observations.

148	\section{Llama-3.1-8B Complete Results}\label{sec:appendix-llama}
149	
150	Table~\ref{tab:llama-full} presents the complete Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct results, complementing the summary in \S\ref{subsec:cross-model}. Three configurations were trained (Base, ThreadGate, LoRA-only) using the same training pipeline as Qwen-2.5-7B (8K UltraChat, 3 epochs, LoRA rank 16). Training required 7.0--7.3 hours per variant on the same GPU.
151	
152	\paragraph{Teacher-forced evaluation.} TF GAR-ours is 0.484 (TG) and 0.481 (LoRA-only), confirming that gating provides zero benefit under teacher forcing on Llama, consistent with the Qwen results (0.50 vs.\ 0.50).
153	
154	\paragraph{Autoregressive evaluation.} AR evaluation uses $N$\,=\,20 mid-turn conversations (turns 3--$T$, excluding the first two turns to avoid initialization effects). The AR GAR distribution is heavy-tailed: the coefficient of variation exceeds 100\% for ThreadGate (mean 0.043, std 0.100), and 5\% of turn-level measurements exhibit sporadic attention spikes (GAR $\geq$ 0.4). We therefore report both mean and median.
155	
156	\paragraph{Gate profile.} Llama's gate profile differs qualitatively from Qwen's: Qwen shows minimum attenuation at early layers (L1\,=\,0.793, L5\,=\,0.797), while Llama shows a V-shaped valley at mid-to-late layers (L25\,=\,0.719, L24\,=\,0.809). Despite this architectural difference, both models converge toward identity under NTP pressure, and the TF-AR gap is comparable (27$\times$ by median for Llama vs.\ 8--17$\times$ for Qwen).

This confirms the mechanism specificity finding: exposure bias selectively disrupts the concentrated last-token attention pattern (GAR-ours) while leaving the diffuse all-token attention (GAR-Dongre) unaffected across both architectures.
177	
178	\section{Additional Visualizations}\label{sec:appendix-viz}
179	
180	This section presents extended visualizations referenced in the main text. Each figure examines a different aspect of the gating behavior and its failure under autoregressive generation.
181	
182	\subsection{Gate Profile Heatmap}
183	
184	Figure~\ref{fig:gate-heatmap} shows the per-layer gate values across all training configurations for both Qwen-2.5-7B (28 layers) and Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers). The key observation is that early layers consistently receive the lowest gate values across all conditions, suggesting that these layers contribute more dispensable computations for the NTP objective. The pattern is remarkably consistent across ThreadGate, Uniform Gate, and PCGrad variants, indicating that gate-value allocation is driven primarily by the NTP loss landscape rather than the GAR auxiliary objective.
185	
186	\begin{figure*}[h]
187	\centering
188	\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{fig_gate_profile_heatmap.pdf}
189	\caption{Per-layer gate values across training for Qwen-2.5-7B (28 layers $\times$ 5 conditions) and Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers $\times$ 1 condition). Early layers (L1, L4--5) consistently receive the lowest gate values across conditions.}
190	\label{fig:gate-heatmap}
191	\end{figure*}
192	
193	\subsection{Cross-Model Gate Profile Comparison}
194	
195	Figure~\ref{fig:gate-crossmodel} compares gate profiles between the two architectures. Qwen-2.5-7B shows minimum gate values at early layers (L1\,=\,0.793, L5\,=\,0.797), suggesting these layers are most amenable to attenuation without disrupting NTP. Llama-3.1-8B instead shows a V-shaped valley at mid-to-late layers (L25\,=\,0.719), indicating that architecturally distinct models learn different layer-importance hierarchies. Both profiles converge toward identity at their respective final layers, consistent with NTP gradient pressure dominating gate optimization at output-adjacent layers.
196	
197	\begin{figure*}[h]
198	\centering
199	\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{fig_gate_profile_crossmodel.pdf}
200	\caption{Side-by-side gate profiles for Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Qwen dips at early layers (L1\,=\,0.793, L5\,=\,0.797), while Llama shows a V-shaped valley at mid-to-late layers (L25\,=\,0.719). Both models learn layer-selective gating but with architecture-dependent patterns.}
201	\label{fig:gate-crossmodel}
202	\end{figure*}
203	
204	\subsection{Per-Turn AR GAR Decay}
205	
206	Figure~\ref{fig:ar-gar-perturn} visualizes the monotonic decay of GAR across conversation turns under autoregressive generation. Qwen base drops 85\% from turn 1 to turn 10; Llama base drops 90\%. The ThreadGate-trained model shows slight elevation in absolute GAR values but follows the same decay pattern, confirming that training-time GAR optimization does not alter the fundamental decay dynamic during generation. This per-turn view complements the aggregate TF-AR gap reported in Table~\ref{tab:four-way}: the gap is not a fixed offset but grows with conversation length, consistent with cumulative exposure bias.
207	
208	\begin{figure*}[h]
209	\centering
210	\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{fig_ar_gar_perturn.pdf}
211	\caption{GAR decays monotonically across turns under autoregressive generation. Qwen base drops 85\% (turn 1$\to$10), Llama base drops 90\%. The ThreadGate-trained model (AR) shows slight elevation but the same decay pattern, confirming that training-time GAR optimization does not transfer to generation.}
212	\label{fig:ar-gar-perturn}
213	\end{figure*}
214	
215	\subsection{Gate Value Distributions}
216	
217	Figure~\ref{fig:gate-distribution} shows the full distribution of per-layer gate values for ThreadGate, Uniform Gate, and PCGrad variants. All three converge to similar distributions (mean $\sim$0.94--0.96, concentrated between 0.9 and 1.0), confirming that the gating mechanism provides minimal modulation regardless of the specific variant. The distributions are right-skewed with a sharp cutoff at 1.0, reflecting NTP pressure pushing gates toward identity.
218	
219	\begin{figure*}[h]
220	\centering
221	\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{fig_gate_distribution.pdf}
222	\caption{Per-layer gate value distributions for ThreadGate, Uniform Gate, and PCGrad variants. All three converge to similar distributions (mean $\sim$0.94--0.96), confirming minimal modulation from the gating mechanism.}
223	\label{fig:gate-distribution}
224	\end{figure*}
225	
226	\subsection{Training Loss Curves}
227	
228	Figure~\ref{fig:training-loss} shows the NTP, GAR, and total loss trajectories during training. GAR loss collapses to near-zero within the first epoch across all variants, indicating rapid convergence of the auxiliary objective under teacher forcing. NTP loss converges normally to ${\sim}$0.93 by epoch 3. The fast GAR convergence is not itself pathological---it indicates successful optimization under the training distribution. The pathology emerges only at the transition to autoregressive generation, where the learned attention patterns fail to transfer.
229	
230	\begin{figure*}[h]
231	\centering
232	\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{fig_training_loss_curves.pdf}
233	\caption{NTP, GAR, and total loss trajectories. GAR loss collapses to near-zero within the first epoch across all variants, while NTP loss converges normally.}
234	\label{fig:training-loss}
235	\end{figure*}

\section{Per-Layer Gate Profile}\label{sec:appendix-gate-profile}

Table~\ref{tab:gate-profile} reports the final per-layer gate values for ThreadGate (seed 123) on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (28 layers). Gate values are averaged across all tokens in the evaluation set. Layers 1 and 5 show the lowest gate values (0.793 and 0.797), indicating these layers are most amenable to attenuation without disrupting NTP. Layers 26--27 converge to $\geq$0.988, consistent with NTP gradient pressure dominating at output-adjacent layers. The mean across all layers is 0.947 ($\sigma$\,=\,0.051).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Per-layer gate values for ThreadGate (seed 123) on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. Min values (L1, L5) in bold.}
\label{tab:gate-profile}
\begin{tabular}{cccccccc}
\toprule
L0 & L1 & L2 & L3 & L4 & L5 & L6 & L7 \\
.883 & \textbf{.793} & .996 & .988 & .984 & \textbf{.797} & .961 & .918 \\
\midrule
L8 & L9 & L10 & L11 & L12 & L13 & L14 & L15 \\
.965 & .934 & .969 & .918 & .926 & .941 & .930 & .965 \\
\midrule
L16 & L17 & L18 & L19 & L20 & L21 & L22 & L23 \\
.941 & .910 & .961 & .965 & .973 & .988 & .969 & .980 \\
\midrule
L24 & L25 & L26 & L27 & \multicolumn{4}{c}{Summary} \\
.980 & .984 & .988 & 1.00 & \multicolumn{4}{c}{$\bar{g}$\,=\,.947, $\sigma$\,=\,.051} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The gate profile exhibits two notable patterns: (1)~a bimodal dip at L1 and L5, suggesting two distinct ``dispensable'' layer clusters in Qwen's architecture; (2)~monotonic increase from L17 to L27, indicating output-adjacent layers are progressively more critical for NTP. Seed 42 produces a similar profile (mean 0.934, min at L3--L5), confirming the pattern is not seed-dependent.

\paragraph{Cross-model comparison.} Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (32 layers) shows a qualitatively different profile: a V-shaped valley at mid-to-late layers (L25\,=\,0.719, L24\,=\,0.809) rather than early-layer dips. Both architectures converge toward identity at output-adjacent layers, but the location of maximum attenuation differs---early for Qwen, late-middle for Llama---suggesting that layer importance hierarchies are architecture-dependent rather than universal.

\section{Scheduled Sampling Implementation}\label{sec:appendix-ss}

Our scheduled sampling implementation follows \citet{bengio2015scheduled} with modifications for multi-turn transformer training:

\paragraph{Sampling schedule.} The model-generated context ratio $\rho$ increases linearly from 0 to 0.5 over 3 epochs. At each training step, a Bernoulli trial with probability $\rho$ determines whether the input prefix is replaced with model-generated tokens. The effective usage rate (29.7--37.1\%) is lower than the nominal schedule due to per-sample Bernoulli variance.

\paragraph{Context generation.} When model-generated context is selected, the model autoregressively generates the assistant turns from the conversation prefix up to the current training position. The generated tokens replace the ground-truth assistant tokens in the input, while user turns remain unchanged. This preserves the multi-turn structure while introducing distributional diversity in the conditioning context.

\paragraph{Training dynamics.} The scheduled sampling variant converges to similar final loss (NTP 0.932 vs.\ 0.930 for standard ThreadGate) but with higher variance in early epochs due to the stochastic context mixing. Gate profiles remain similar (mean 0.953 vs.\ 0.947, min at L4 vs.\ L1), indicating that scheduled sampling does not fundamentally alter gate optimization but rather improves the robustness of the learned attention patterns to distributional shift. Training time increases approximately 60\% due to the autoregressive generation overhead during training (6.5h vs.\ 6.0h on Qwen; 10.8h for the seed-123 variant which uses a longer schedule).

\section{Computational Cost Analysis}\label{sec:appendix-cost}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Computational cost across training configurations. All experiments use a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (102\,GB VRAM).}
\label{tab:cost}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Config} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Time (h)} & \textbf{VRAM} & \textbf{Overhead} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\emph{Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct}} \\
LoRA-only & 4.2M & 6.0 & 42\,GB & baseline \\
ThreadGate & 4.3M & 6.0 & 43\,GB & $+$57K \\
\;+\,PCGrad & 4.3M & 7.2 & 43\,GB & $+$20\% \\
Uniform Gate & 4.3M & 6.0 & 43\,GB & $+$57K \\
SS (s42) & 4.3M & 6.5 & 43\,GB & $+$8\% \\
SS (s123) & 4.3M & 10.8 & 43\,GB & $+$80\% \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\emph{Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct}} \\
LoRA-only & 4.2M & 7.0 & 45\,GB & baseline \\
ThreadGate & 4.3M & 7.3 & 46\,GB & $+$65K \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Parameter overhead.} ThreadGate adds ${\sim}$57K gate parameters for Qwen-2.5-7B (28 layers $\times$ 2K per gate MLP) and ${\sim}$65K for Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers), representing $<$0.001\% of the base model. LoRA adapters (rank 16, targeting $q$/$v$ projections) contribute 4.2M parameters across both architectures.

\paragraph{Training time.} Standard variants (ThreadGate, Uniform Gate, LoRA-only) train in 6.0--7.3 hours. PCGrad adds ${\sim}$20\% overhead due to the per-step gradient projection computation. Scheduled sampling overhead varies: seed 42 adds only 8\% (6.5h) due to efficient batched generation, while seed 123 adds 80\% (10.8h) because of a longer generation schedule. The difference is due to the extended AR generation schedule in the seed 123 variant.

\paragraph{Inference overhead.} Gate computation at inference time is negligible: a single 32$\to$64$\to$1 MLP forward pass per layer adds $<$0.1\% latency. $\beta$-steering requires identifying goal tokens (a one-time operation per conversation) and adding a constant bias to attention logits, with zero additional parameters.

\section{Qualitative Steering Examples}\label{sec:appendix-examples}

Table~\ref{tab:examples} illustrates the effect of $\beta$-steering on model behavior in a 4-turn conversation where the system prompt instructs ``Always respond in exactly three bullet points.''

\begin{table*}[h]
\centering\small
\caption{Qualitative effect of $\beta$-steering on instruction following across conversation turns. System prompt: ``Always respond in exactly three bullet points.'' ThreadGate checkpoint, 4-turn conversation.}
\label{tab:examples}
\begin{tabular}{c p{5.5cm} p{5.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Turn} & \textbf{$\beta$\,=\,0 (unsteered)} & \textbf{$\beta$\,=\,3 (steered)} \\
\midrule
1 & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic \\
2 & \checkmark~Three bullet points, relevant & \checkmark~Three bullet points, relevant \\
3 & $\sim$~Four bullet points, partially on-topic & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic \\
4 & \texttimes~Free-form paragraph, no bullets & \checkmark~Three bullet points, on-topic \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

The pattern is consistent with the GAR decay analysis: unsteered models progressively lose attention to the system-prompt constraint, leading to format violations at later turns. Steering maintains goal-token attention, preserving instruction compliance. Content constraints (e.g., ``never mention X'') show the largest improvement (+23.8\,pp at $\beta$\,=\,3; Table~\ref{tab:ir-results}), while format constraints that are more procedural show no change, consistent with the hypothesis that GAR captures attention to semantic goal content rather than procedural formatting rules.

This confirms the mechanism specificity finding: exposure bias selectively disrupts the concentrated last-token attention pattern (GAR-ours) while leaving the diffuse all-token attention (GAR-Dongre) unaffected across both architectures.

\paragraph{Training details.} Llama variants used the same pipeline as Qwen: 8K UltraChat conversations, LoRA rank 16 targeting $q$/$v$ projections, 3 epochs. \paragraph{Phase 1 diagnostics.} Before fine-tuning, we confirmed that Llama exhibits the same goal attention decay as Qwen. Base model GAR decays from 0.026 (turn 1) to 0.003 (turn 10), a 90\% decline. toolUseResult.newString:
\paragraph{GAR-Dongre cross-model comparison.} GAR-Dongre shows negligible distribution shift on Llama (AR/TF ratio 1.002$\times$), compared to 1.28$\times$ on Qwen. This confirms the mechanism specificity finding: exposure bias selectively disrupts the concentrated last-token attention pattern (GAR-ours) while leaving the diffuse all-token attention (GAR-Dongre) unaffected across both architectures.

\paragraph{Training details.} Llama variants used the same pipeline as Qwen: 8K UltraChat conversations, LoRA rank 16 targeting $q$/$v$ projections, 3 epochs. Training loss converged to 0.929 (LoRA-only) and 0.934 (ThreadGate); the slight difference is attributable to the additional GAR loss component. Wall-clock time was 7.0h (LoRA-only) and 7.3h (ThreadGate), approximately 17\% longer than Qwen due to Llama's larger intermediate dimension (14336 vs.\ 18944).

\paragraph{Phase 1 diagnostics.} Before fine-tuning, we confirmed that Llama exhibits the same goal attention decay as Qwen. Base model GAR decays from 0.026 (turn 1) to 0.003 (turn 10), a 90\% decline. This is steeper than Qwen's 70.8\% decline, suggesting that attention decay may be more severe in Llama's architecture despite its larger head count (32 vs.\ 28 KV heads).

\paragraph{Training time.} Standard variants (ThreadGate, Uniform Gate, LoRA-only) train in 6.0--7.3 hours. PCGrad adds ${\sim}$20\% overhead due to the per-step gradient projection computation. Scheduled sampling overhead varies: seed 42 adds only 8\% (6.5h) due to efficient batched generation, while seed 123 adds 80\% (10.8h) because of a longer generation schedule. The difference is due to the extended AR generation schedule in the seed 123 variant.
